newsitem.title: USA: Ill. judge rejects incinerator subsidy lawsuits.
newsitem.headline: Ill. judge rejects incinerator subsidy lawsuits.

text.p: An Illinois judge has dismissed lawsuits by the owners of partly-bond financed waste-to-energy incinerators, ruling that they could pursue their challenges to the repeal of a state subsidy only in a court of claims.

"These lawsuits, boiled down to basics, are indeed suits against the state," Cook County Judge Robert Boharic found Friday. "Plaintiffs seek the huge subsidies promised under the prior law from the state treasury."
As a result, the developers of incinerators in Ford Heights, Robbins and Fulton may challenge the legislative repeal of a state subsidy for their benefit in the court of claims only, Boharic ruled.
"We are extremely pleased with this decision," said Alexander Ewing, staff attorney for the Environmental Law & Policy Center. "This is a significant setback for the incinerators."
The incinerator owners could appeal the ruling of the state court judge's decision, or file a new challenge in the Court of Claims, which is not considered a favorable jurisdiction for such a case.

CGE Ford Heights, Foster Wheeler Corp and CGE Fulton had developed incinerator plans based on a state subsidy that would allow them to charge public utilities a higher rate for the electricity they generated in the waste-to-energy facilities.
The General Assembly repealed that subsidy in 1996, however, leading to multiple challenges in state court and U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.
The incinerator in Robbins was completed, has operated on a temporary construction permit and is currently shutdown while awaiting its permanent operating license.
Developers moth-balled the already completed Ford Heights facility when lawmakers repealed the subsidy.
The Ford Heights facility was partly financed by $80 million of tax-exempt bonds, Robbins $320 million and the yet-to-be-built facility in Fulton with $84.6 million.
In the consolidated state cases before Boharic, incinerator developers contended that the retroactive repeal of the subsidy violated contract law and both the Illinois and U.S. Constitutions.
Attorneys representing the state brought motions to dismiss, contending that it has sovereign immunity from such claims.
"In this court's opinion, plaintiffs truly seek to control the actions of the state and impose liability on the state," Boharic wrote in his 15-page decision.
Boharic also rejected contentions from the Robbins incinerator plaintiffs that barring their pursuit of a challenge in the circuit court would violate the Illinois and U.S. Constitutions.
A separate challenge to the repeal, filed by Polsky Energy Corp, remains pending in another state jurisdiction. An appeal taken from the dismissal of a federal lawsuit also remains pending.
Supports of the incinerators have made several attempts to reinstate the subsidy in some form during the current legislative session.
